pass_a_gloss:
The blessed David [said] 'I said in my ecstasy: Every man is a liar;' the same also would become a word concerning God and us and about all the others; such as concerning righteousness, for anyone would indeed say and not outside of the word: Let God be righteous, but every man unrighteous. If, however, our unrighteousness establishes God's righteousness. The pretext of such a slander has come about from here: after the return from Babylon, the sons of Israel, having been commanded by Cyrus to rebuild the temple and to fulfill vows and to bring sacrifices, have become compliant, pretending poverty and the hardship from the captivity; by this, they were being made wise through moderate educations, through scarcities of fruits and rains; but being unshakeable toward such blows, they were indeed blessing the foreigners and those not serving God as living in good cheer, and they were saying that those were more blessed than themselves; and indeed the prophet Malachi spoke toward them, 'You have made your words heavy upon me, says the Lord, and said: In what way have we spoken against you? Say, says the vain one serving God, and what more [is there], that we kept his guardrails, and because we went humbly before the face of the Lord Pantokrator? And now we bless strangers, and they build houses.' They withstood God and were saved. These things the ones fearing the Lord spoke, each toward his neighbor; and the Lord attended and heard. Because of this reason, he says, some were inclined to say the Jews: Let us do evil so that good things might come.

[p1] Having said the judgment [is] a full measure of righteousness, or of the Jews reproaching those things, that is, of those daring to say: 'Let us do evils so that good things might come.' [p2] But now apart from law the righteousness of God has been revealed. [p3] I know that it has been written concerning certain [men], that 'they were both righteous, walking in the commandments and judgments of Christ, blameless,' and the blessed Paul said, that he himself also 'according to righteousness in the law has become blameless.' But the one [is] blameless in this, [he] has not yet done those things through which he will be bright and without reproach; [p4] and indeed the blessed Paul said again, how he reckoned all things in the law as loss and as equal refuse; [p5] and again he seeks 'the excellence of the knowledge of Christ.' And again the law condemns those transgressing; [p6] by this indeed he says, 'For if in the ministry of condemnation there is glory, much more abounds the ministry of righteousness in glory;' and since there is a greater commandment in it, it is necessary in some way even to trip up the precise law-keeper and to establish him as a transgressor of the law. [p7] And that the noble disciples have truly and clearly judged [him] to be a burden; [p8] for they were saying, 'Now therefore what are you testing God, to lay a yoke upon the necks of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?'
pass_b_english: The blessed David said that in his ecstasy, he proclaimed that every man is a liar, a statement that also applies to God, to us, and to all others.
For instance, when it comes to righteousness, it can be said, without straying from the truth, that God is righteous, while every man is unrighteous, as stated in Romans 3:4.
If our unrighteousness serves to establish God's righteousness, then this idea has given rise to a pretext for slander, which originated from the time when the sons of Israel returned from Babylon.

After their return, the sons of Israel were commanded by Cyrus to rebuild the temple, fulfill their vows, and offer sacrifices, but they became complacent, pretending to be poor and suffering from the hardships of captivity, and were being tempered by moderate educations and the scarcity of fruits and rains, which made them wise.

Despite these challenges, they remained unshakeable and even blessed the foreigners and those who did not serve God, as if they were living in prosperity, and claimed that these people were more blessed than themselves.

The prophet Malachi spoke out against them, saying, 'You have made your words heavy upon me, says the Lord, and have said: In what way have we spoken against you?' (Malachi 2:4), and, 'Say, and what more is there, that we kept His guardrails and went humbly before the face of the Lord Almighty? And now we bless strangers, and they are building houses!' (Malachi 3:14-15).
They withstood God and were saved, and those who feared the Lord discussed these things among themselves, with each one speaking to his neighbor, and the Lord listened and responded.

Because of this, some Jews were inclined to say, daring to presume that they could say, 'Let us do evil so that good things might come,' having declared that the judgment is a full measure of righteousness, and addressing those who were reproaching them for such ideas.

But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been revealed, and it is known that certain men were considered righteous, walking in the commandments and judgments of Christ, blameless, and the blessed Paul said that he himself had also become blameless according to the righteousness that is in the law.

However, being blameless in this regard does not mean that one has already performed the deeds that will make him bright and without reproach, and the blessed Paul said again that he had reckoned all things in the law as loss and as equal refuse, seeking instead the excellence of the knowledge of Christ.

The law, however, continues to condemn those who transgress, and it is clear that if there is glory in the ministry of condemnation, then the ministry of righteousness must abound even more in glory, as stated in 2 Corinthians 3:9.
Since there is a greater commandment within the law, it is inevitable that even the most precise law-keeper will stumble and become a transgressor of the law in some way.

The noble disciples have truly and clearly judged the law to be a burden, saying, 'Now then, why are you testing God by placing a yoke upon the necks of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?' (Acts 15:10).
